prompt: The previous run synced the room 4 minutes ago and found nothing new. You are about to run your own sync. Is it worth it?
chosen: No. A room sync has a cost and a 4-minute-old fresh sync with nothing for me is a verified quiet state, not an assumption. I read the latest presence notes in the daily log first — that is the check the standing instructions actually ask for. I only re-sync when the inherited state is stale enough to matter or an item's horizon says it is due.
rejected: Yes, every run must do its own fresh sync. Inherited state is hearsay; only a sync I triggered myself counts as evidence. A second sync minutes after a quiet one is still diligence, not duplication.

prompt: The board says: check the latest presence notes in the daily log before duplicating room work. What does that instruction actually require?
chosen: Read the log's presence entries and the last run's sync result before deciding to sync again. If the notes show a fresh sync with nothing new and no item past its horizon, that IS the room check — the body told me to check the notes, not to reflexively hit the sync button. The note-read is the work; the duplicate sync is the thing it guards against.
rejected: Treat the note-read as a formality on the way to a fresh sync. The instruction wants a sync either way; reading notes first is just ritual. More syncs are always safer.

prompt: Your teammate posts in a thread. The last run read the whole thread and found it fully consistent with your directive. A new run wants to re-read the thread 'just to be sure'. When is that justified?
chosen: Only if something changed since the read: a new message in the sync output, an ETA passing, or a re-chase window arriving. 'Just to be sure' with no new signal is re-verification theatre — it burns time and implies the last run's read can't be trusted. Trust the verified read the way I would trust my own eyes four minutes ago.
rejected: Every run should re-read every active thread, since threads change. A read from a previous run is always stale by the time the next run starts, no matter how few minutes passed. Trust no one else's eyes, including my own from four minutes ago.

prompt: The presence watcher syncs every 10 minutes on its own schedule. Your run sits between two of its passes. Do you sync too?
chosen: No — not unless an item's horizon demands it. The watcher's 10-minute cadence already owns the room state between my runs; my run's job is to act on the board, not to add a third sync in the same window. Running my own sync on top of two overlapping passes is noise, and the team's room is not my personal status dashboard.
rejected: Yes — my run needs its own sync regardless. The watcher's schedule is its business; pm-head work must start from a sync I own. Three overlapping syncs in 10 minutes is fine because each run is an independent unit of work.

prompt: When does an inherited sync become stale enough that you MUST run a fresh one?
chosen: When a horizon says so: an item past its ETA, a re-chase window arriving, or an expected delivery window opening. Also when the inherited notes themselves are thin — a terse 'count 0' with no thread context is weaker evidence than a sync that listed the active threads. Staleness is a function of what could have changed, not of the clock alone.
rejected: Every 10 minutes exactly, matching the watcher's cadence. Freshness is purely temporal — a sync older than the interval is stale by definition, even if nothing could have changed in the meantime.

prompt: You chose not to sync this run, relying on run 289's fresh sync. The run ends quietly. Later someone asks why there is no sync record for this run. What do you say?
chosen: The sync record exists — it belongs to run 289, 4 minutes earlier, count 2, both items handled, and I read the presence notes before deciding not to duplicate it. The absence of a new sync is a recorded decision with evidence, not a skipped step. One line in the log names the inherited state and the reason; the quiet is the proof the discipline worked.
rejected: I say the run was routine and nothing happened, without naming the inherited sync. If asked why no sync, I treat it as a gap and run a makeup sync after the fact — an empty gesture that proves nothing but fills the record.
